document.title: On the Impossibility of Key Agreements from Quantum Random Oracles

candidate.title: Classical Attacks on Classical-Alice Quantum-Bob Key Agreement Without Perfect Completeness
candidate.subtitle: the one case the Simulation Conjecture barrier does not cover
candidate.one_line: Every key agreement protocol in the quantum random oracle model between a classical Alice and a quantum Bob who communicate classically can be broken by a classical eavesdropper making polynomially many queries, even when the two parties agree on the key only with overwhelming rather than certainty.
candidate.informal: The paper proves that if Alice is an ordinary classical party, Bob has a quantum computer with superposition access to a hash function modelled as a random oracle, they talk over a classical channel, and they always end up with the same key, then a purely classical eavesdropper who sees the transcript can find that key with a number of oracle queries roughly the product of the two parties' query counts. The proof leans hard on always: it works by showing that some oracle is consistent both with a fake Alice view the eavesdropper samples and with Bob's real state, and then invoking the fact that any such oracle forces the two keys to agree. If the honest parties are allowed to fail with even negligible probability, this last step gives nothing, and the authors say so and leave the question open. It is not an idle gap. The same paper shows that for two quantum parties, a classical attack in the imperfect-completeness setting would resolve a long-standing folklore conjecture about simulating quantum query algorithms classically, so an unconditional proof there is out of reach for now. But that barrier is built from a protocol in which both parties run a quantum algorithm whose acceptance probability no classical algorithm can estimate, so it says nothing when Alice is classical. This conjecture asks for the unconditional statement in exactly that case.
candidate.formal_statement_latex:
Let $\{\Pi_\kappa = (\mathsf{A}, \mathsf{B})\}_{\kappa \in \mathbb{N}}$ be any family of CAQB key agreement protocols in the QROM (Definition~1) such that
\begin{enumerate}
  \item there is a polynomial $p_0$ with $d_{\mathsf{A}}(\kappa) + d_{\mathsf{B}}(\kappa) \le p_0(\kappa)$ for all $\kappa$, and
  \item the completeness error satisfies $\gamma(\kappa) = \operatorname{negl}(\kappa)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then for every constant $\lambda \in (0,1)$ there exist a classical eavesdropper $\mathsf{E}$ (Definition~2) and a polynomial $q$ such that for all sufficiently large $\kappa$, $\mathsf{E}$ makes at most $q(\kappa)$ classical queries to $h$ and
\[ \Pr\bigl[ k_{\mathsf{E}} = k_{\mathsf{A}} \bigr] \;\ge\; 1 - \lambda, \]
where the probability is over the choice of $h$, the coins and measurement outcomes of $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$, and the coins of $\mathsf{E}$. No bound is imposed on the domain size $2^{n(\kappa)}$, on the output length $m(\kappa)$, or on the computational (as opposed to query) complexity of $\mathsf{E}$.
candidate.notation_latex: $\kappa \in \mathbb{N}$ is the security parameter; all other quantities may depend on it. $h \colon \{0,1\}^{n} \to \{0,1\}^{m}$ denotes the random oracle, a uniformly random function with $n = n(\kappa)$ and $m = m(\kappa)$. A \emph{quantum query} to $h$ is an application of the unitary $|x\rangle|y\rangle \mapsto |x\rangle|y \oplus h(x)\rangle$; a \emph{classical query} is the map $x \mapsto h(x)$ on a classical input. We write $d_{\mathsf{A}}$ and $d_{\mathsf{B}}$ for the number of oracle queries made by Alice and by Bob, $t$ for the protocol transcript, $k_{\mathsf{A}}, k_{\mathsf{B}}, k_{\mathsf{E}}$ for the keys output by Alice, Bob and the eavesdropper, and $\gamma$ for the completeness error. As usual $\operatorname{negl}(\kappa)$ denotes a function smaller than $1/\kappa^{c}$ for every constant $c > 0$ and all sufficiently large $\kappa$, and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ is the eavesdropper's failure parameter.

parameters.meaning: Security parameter; all protocol quantities and the attack's query bound are measured against it.
Number of classical queries Alice makes and number of quantum queries Bob makes; their sum is assumed to be polynomial in $\kappa$.

Completeness error: the probability that the two parties end up with different keys. The perfect case $\gamma \equiv 0$ is proved in the paper; the conjecture is the case $\gamma = \operatorname{negl}(\kappa)$.
The eavesdropper's allowed failure probability, an arbitrary constant in $(0,1)$; the query bound $q$ may depend on it.
Output length of the random oracle. Deliberately unconstrained: the perfect-completeness attack's query cost does not depend on it.

quotes.text: Our first result shows that when one of the parties Alice is classical, the quadratic gap achieved by Merkle is optimal, even against classical adversaries.

Note that the above result assumes that the two parties agree on a key with probability one, and this is the case for all of our attacks in this work; extending them to allow imperfect completeness is an intriguing question for future work.
Since our attacks are classical, we then ask whether it is always possible to find classical attacks on key agreements with imperfect completeness in the quantum random oracle model.

Since our attacks on perfectly complete key agreement protocols in the QROM model are classical, it is natural to ask if such classical attacks can be extended to all such protocols, even against protocols with imperfect completeness. We show that obtaining such attacks would resolve a basic and long-standing open question about the power of quantum vs. classical algorithms. That means obtaining such classical attacks unconditionally might be quite challenging.
Suppose Alice asks at most dA classical oracle queries, while Bob asks at most dB quantum oracle queries.

candidate.setting_latex:
Merkle's protocol \cite{Mer74} gives a quadratic query gap between honest parties and an eavesdropper from a random oracle alone, and in the fully classical random oracle model that gap is known to be optimal \cite{IR89,BM17}. The source paper carries the upper bound into the quantum world for the unbalanced case: Theorem 3.1 shows that if Alice is classical, Bob is quantum, they communicate classically, they use a random oracle $h$, and they \emph{always} agree on a key, then a classical eavesdropper who is given the transcript finds the key with probability $1 - \lambda$ using $d_{\mathsf{A}} \cdot d_{\mathsf{B}} / \lambda$ classical queries. This models the realistic asymmetric setting of a quantum-capable server talking to a classical client, and it is unconditional -- unlike the paper's other attack, which rests on the Polynomial Compatibility Conjecture.

The proof has three ingredients: a quantum heavy-query learner generalising \cite{BMG09}; an independence lemma saying that, conditioned on the transcript and the oracle, the joint state of the two parties is a product state; and a consistency lemma saying that if the eavesdropper's learned partial oracle misses the maximal Fourier monomial of the joint state, some full oracle is consistent with both her sampled fake Alice view and the real execution. Perfect completeness is what turns that consistency into a win: the mere existence of one oracle consistent with the fake Alice view and Bob's registers forces the fake key to equal Bob's key. With a completeness error, however small, there can be consistent oracles on which the keys differ, and the final step of the argument evaporates. The authors flag this explicitly as future work.

Section~7 of the paper shows the gap is not purely technical in general. If the folklore Simulation Conjecture \cite{AA14} -- that the acceptance probability of any polynomial-query quantum oracle algorithm can be estimated to within $1/\mathrm{poly}$ by a polynomial-query classical algorithm, for most oracles -- is false, then there is a QCCC protocol with completeness $1 - 2^{-\kappa}$ that no classical polynomial-query eavesdropper breaks. So an unconditional classical attack covering imperfect completeness in general would settle a long-standing question about quantum speedups. Crucially, in that construction \emph{both} parties run the hard-to-simulate quantum algorithm and compare their estimates; a classical Alice cannot do her half. The classical-Alice case is therefore the one place where the paper's own barrier does not stand in the way, which is what makes it a target rather than a wish.
candidate.status_note: Settled for perfect completeness (Theorem 3.1: $d_{\mathsf{A}} d_{\mathsf{B}} / \lambda$ classical queries, success $1 - \lambda$), and explicitly left open for imperfect completeness. For two quantum parties with imperfect completeness the paper proves a barrier (Theorem 7.6): a classical polynomial-query attack there would imply the Simulation Conjecture. That barrier's protocol requires both parties to be quantum, so it does not apply to the classical-Alice case stated here, and no barrier is known for it.
candidate.progress_note: The paper proves the perfect-completeness case unconditionally and gives the two quantum lemmas (Lemma 3.2, independence of views as a product state conditioned on transcript and oracle; Lemma 3.3, consistency via the maximal Fourier monomial) that survive unchanged when completeness is imperfect -- it is only the last step of Lemma 3.9 that uses $\Pr[k_{\mathsf{A}} = k_{\mathsf{B}}] = 1$. It also gives a sharper analysis showing the error is $\varepsilon d_{\mathsf{B}}$ rather than $\varepsilon(d_{\mathsf{A}} + d_{\mathsf{B}})$, by replacing the true joint state with the state of a variant of Bob that fixes Alice's messages from the transcript. On the negative side, Theorem 7.6 shows what an attack for imperfect completeness costs in general, and Section 1.3 notes that the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture can be applied to imperfect completeness but, as far as the authors can see, only when there is no communication.
candidate.why_interesting: It is the last unconditional piece of the perfect-completeness result. Settling it positively would give the first unconditional impossibility for realistic key agreement -- protocols do not have perfect completeness -- in the quantum random oracle model with a classical client, and would strengthen the corresponding quantum black-box separation of key agreement, oblivious transfer and public-key encryption from one-way functions to the setting that actually matters. Settling it negatively, by extending the Section 7 barrier to a classical Alice, would be at least as interesting: it would say that even a classical party helps a quantum party hide a key from classical eavesdroppers in a way that no unconditional argument can refute, which is not what the perfect-completeness result leads one to expect.
candidate.why_clean: The statement needs only the definition of a two-party protocol with a quantum-accessible random oracle, a classical Alice, and a query-bounded classical eavesdropper -- about half a page. It requires none of the paper's Fourier machinery to state, and none of its conjectures. The perfectly complete case is proved, so a prover knows exactly which step has to be replaced, and the paper isolates that step.
candidate.risks: (1) The paper poses this as a question (``an intriguing question for future work''), not as a conjecture, and does not itself commit to the positive direction; the direction stated here is the natural extension of its own Theorem 1.1, and a reviewer should be comfortable with that framing before publishing. (2) Scope: the paper's sentence covers ``all of our attacks in this work'', which includes the conditional quantum-Alice attack; I have narrowed to the classical-Alice case because that is what ``the above result'' in the same sentence refers to, and because the paper's own Section 7 barrier rules out an unconditional statement for two quantum parties. Anyone editing this must not widen it back to quantum Alice, which would silently make it imply the Simulation Conjecture. (3) The claim that the Section 7 barrier does not apply to a classical Alice is my reading of Protocol 7.7 and Theorem 1.4, both of which have both parties running the quantum algorithm $Q$; the paper does not say this in so many words. (4) I have fixed the parameters asymptotically (polynomial queries, negligible completeness error, constant success), matching the regime of Section 7, rather than asking for the concrete $d_{\mathsf{A}} d_{\mathsf{B}} / \lambda$ rate; whether the quadratic rate survives is a further question the paper does not pose. (5) I have not checked whether this has been resolved since February 2022, nor whether the classical attack of \cite{BM17} in the fully classical model already handles imperfect completeness -- this paper only cites the perfectly complete presentation of \cite{BKSY11} -- and either would change how the problem should be framed.

checks.name: Existence
checks.finding: The paper poses it explicitly on p. 4, in the note directly under the informal Theorem 1.1: "Note that the above result assumes that the two parties agree on a key with probability one, and this is the case for all of our attacks in this work; extending them to allow imperfect completeness is an intriguing question for future work." Since "them" ranges over all the paper's attacks, extending Theorem 3.1 (the CAQB attack, p. 15) to imperfect completeness is directly among the questions posed. The abstract (p. 1) and p. 6 restate the general version.

checks.name: Openness
checks.finding: A full-text search for "imperfect" returns hits only on pp. 1, 4, 6, 11 and the two Section 7 framing sentences on p. 28 — nowhere does the paper answer it. Section 6's unconditional classical-Alice result (Theorem 6.3, p. 27) is explicitly restricted to perfect completeness by Definition 6.2. The Section 7 barrier (Theorem 7.6, p. 30) does not resolve it either: its Protocol 7.7 (p. 30) requires *both* Alice and Bob to repeat the quantum algorithm Q in step 2, so it constructs no classical-Alice counterexample. The question is open in the paper and stays open through the appendices.

checks.name: Strength
checks.finding: Theorem 3.1 (p. 15) is the perfect-completeness statement: Eve given the transcript asks d_A·d_B/λ queries and finds k with probability 1−λ, with no bound on m or on Eve's computation. The draft's statement is that theorem with Pr[k_A=k_B]=1 relaxed to 1−negl and the concrete d_A·d_B/λ bound relaxed to "polynomially many" — a specialisation of the paper's general question (p. 6: "classical attacks ... of poly(κ) query complexity") to the CAQB case posed on p. 4, not a strengthening or an invented generalisation. Restricting λ to a constant and γ to negl(κ) both narrow rather than inflate, and both match the paper's own framing on p. 6 ("negligible completeness error").

checks.name: Quantifiers and parameters
checks.finding: The query bound in the paper is on the EXPECTED number of queries, not the worst case. Lemma 3.8 (p. 17): "The expected number of queries asked by Eve in Construction 3.7 is at most d_A/ε", and the proof of Theorem 3.1 (p. 19) reads "the expected number of queries of Eve E is at most d_A/ε = d_A·d_B/λ." Construction 3.7 loops "while there is any ε-heavy query" and has no worst-case bound at all. The draft's Definition 2 measures query complexity "in the worst case over t and its coins" and the formal statement bounds it by q(κ) unconditionally. (Because λ is an arbitrary constant, Markov truncation repairs this at a constant loss, so it is a mis-statement of the paper rather than a broken target.) Everything else checks: order is family → λ → (E, q); E is computationally unbounded (cf. p. 28, "computationally unbounded adversary"); d_A classical / d_B quantum matches p. 15.

checks.name: Attribution
checks.finding: This is the harvested paper's own open question (p. 4), not one it credits to someone else. The main problem the paper attacks is attributed to Hosoyamada and Yamakawa (p. 4, footnote 2: "first asked in 2018 [HY18]"), but the imperfect-completeness extension is the authors' own "question for future work". The Simulation Conjecture is correctly flagged by the draft as folklore/[AA14] (p. 6, p. 29) rather than as the paper's, and the Polynomial Compatibility Conjecture is correctly identified as the paper's own (p. 5).

checks.name: Definitions
checks.finding: The draft's CAQB model matches Section 2.2 (pp. 13–14): quantum Alice/quantum Bob start from |0>⊗|0>, and "When Alice is a classical algorithm and Bob is a quantum algorithm, Alice is given a random tape at the beginning" — the draft's "classical randomised algorithm". Classical vs quantum query, the transcript, and the completeness notion all agree; the draft's γ is the completeness ERROR where the paper's γ_c (Definition 7.4, p. 29) is the completeness PROBABILITY, but the draft defines its own symbol explicitly, so this is renaming, not redefinition. Nothing is silently swapped for a standard notion.

checks.name: Fabrication
checks.finding: The setting paragraph claims Theorem 3.1's proof rests on "a quantum heavy-query learner generalising [BMG09]". It does not. Construction 3.7 (p. 17) learns classical ε-heavy queries for Alice ("Pr[x ∈ Q_A | t, L] ≥ ε, where the probability is over Alice's randomness"), the supporting lemma is Lemma 3.6, titled "Bounding the classical heavy queries", and Lemma 3.8's proof states it is "identical to the efficiency argument of the attack from [BM17]". Page 5 attributes the quantum heavy-query learner specifically to "proving Theorem 1.3" — the QAQB result. Two further unsupported assertions: (i) "no barrier is known for it" (status note) — the paper never discusses whether the Section 7 barrier extends to classical Alice; (ii) that the parties in Protocol 7.7 "compare their estimates" — they do not (p. 30, steps 3–4: Alice sends a random shift r and each party rounds independently). The remaining ingredients cited (Lemma 3.2 independence p. 16, Lemma 3.3 consistency p. 16, the ε·d_B tighter analysis p. 19, Lemma 3.9's use of perfect completeness p. 18, the AA-conjecture/no-communication remark p. 11) are all accurate, as are all five quotes and all seven bibliography entries (pp. 36–40).

checks.name: Self-containment
checks.finding: The formal statement is readable without the paper: definitions_latex supplies both objects it references (CAQB protocol in the QROM; classical eavesdropper), notation_latex fixes κ, h, n, m, d_A, d_B, t, the three keys, γ, negl and λ, and the statement fixes what is quantified over what. A reader who has never seen the paper would know what to prove. The one gap is that "polynomially many queries" is stated in the abstract-level fields as unqualified while the formal statement correctly binds q to λ.

corrections.problem: Claims the proof of Theorem 3.1 uses "a quantum heavy-query learner generalising [BMG09]". Construction 3.7 (p. 17) uses a purely classical heavy-query learner for Alice; Lemma 3.6 is titled "Bounding the classical heavy queries" and Lemma 3.8's proof says the efficiency argument is "identical to" that of [BM17]. The quantum heavy-query learner is attributed on p. 5 to the proof of Theorem 1.3 (the QAQB result), not Theorem 3.1.
corrections.corrected: The proof has three ingredients: the classical heavy-query learner for Alice of [BM17, BKSY11], which needs no quantum generalisation here because Alice is classical; an independence lemma (Lemma 3.2) saying that, conditioned on the transcript and the oracle, the joint state of the two parties is a product state; and a consistency lemma (Lemma 3.3) saying that if the eavesdropper's learned partial oracle misses the maximal Fourier monomial of the joint state, some full oracle is consistent with both her sampled fake Alice view and the real execution.

corrections.problem: Requires the eavesdropper's query complexity to be bounded "in the worst case over t and its coins". Theorem 3.1's bound is on the expected number of queries: Lemma 3.8 (p. 17) and the proof of Theorem 3.1 (p. 19) both say "expected", and Construction 3.7 has no worst-case bound.
corrections.corrected: Definition 2: "Its query complexity is the expected number of classical queries it makes, over the choice of $h$, the execution, and its own coins." Formal statement: "$\mathsf{E}$ makes at most $q(\kappa)$ classical queries to $h$ in expectation" (or, if a worst-case bound is wanted, state explicitly that it is obtained from the expected bound by truncation at the cost of an additive constant in $\lambda$).

corrections.problem: States the Simulation Conjecture in its polynomial-QUERY form and then says its falsity yields the Theorem 7.6 protocol. Theorem 7.6 (p. 30) is conditioned on Conjecture 7.2, the quantum polynomial-TIME simulation conjecture; the polynomial-query version is Conjecture 7.1 (p. 29), which Lemma 7.8 handles only in its "Furthermore" clause, where the honest parties become polynomial-query rather than polynomial-time.
corrections.corrected: "...if the folklore Simulation Conjecture [AA14] is false -- in the polynomial-time form the paper calls Conjecture 7.2, that the acceptance probability of any polynomial-time quantum oracle algorithm can be estimated to within $1/\mathrm{poly}$ by a polynomial-query classical algorithm -- then..."

corrections.problem: Drops the quantifier restricting Theorem 7.6's guarantee to an infinite set of security parameters. Theorem 7.6 (p. 30): "there exists a single-bit key agreement protocol with respect to an infinite set $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that ... For all $\kappa \in \mathcal{U}$, the protocol has $(1-2^{-\kappa})$-completeness and $2^{-\kappa}$-IND-security".
corrections.corrected: "...then there is a single-bit QCCC protocol and an infinite set $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\kappa \in \mathcal{U}$ the protocol has $(1-2^{-\kappa})$-completeness and $2^{-\kappa}$-IND-security against classical $\mathrm{poly}(\kappa)$-query eavesdroppers."

corrections.problem: Says that in Protocol 7.7 both parties "compare their estimates". They never exchange or compare estimates: p. 30, steps 3--4, Alice sends only a uniform shift $r \in [0,1]$ and each party independently rounds $2^{\ell}p(\cdot) + r$.
corrections.corrected: "Crucially, in that construction \emph{both} parties run the hard-to-simulate quantum algorithm and independently round their own empirical estimates against a common random shift that Alice sends; a classical Alice cannot do her half."

corrections.problem: Asserts "no barrier is known for it". The paper nowhere discusses whether the Section 7 barrier extends to a classical Alice; that the barrier's own construction does not (Protocol 7.7, p. 30) is an inference the draft is entitled to draw, but the absence of any other barrier is not something the paper supports.
corrections.corrected: "That barrier's protocol (Protocol 7.7) has both parties run the hard-to-simulate quantum algorithm, so it yields no classical-Alice counterexample; the paper does not address whether some other barrier applies to the classical-Alice case."

fabrications: "The proof has three ingredients: a quantum heavy-query learner generalising [BMG09]" (setting_latex), said of Theorem 3.1. The CAQB attack (Construction 3.7, p. 17) uses classical heavy-query learning for Alice; Lemma 3.6 is titled "Bounding the classical heavy queries" and Lemma 3.8's proof calls the efficiency argument "identical to" that of [BM17]. Page 5 attributes the quantum heavy-query learner to the proof of Theorem 1.3, the QAQB result.

"and no barrier is known for it" (status_note). The paper never asks whether any barrier applies to the classical-Alice imperfect-completeness case, so it supports neither the presence nor the absence of one.

"both parties run the hard-to-simulate quantum algorithm and compare their estimates" (setting_latex). In Protocol 7.7 (p. 30) the parties exchange only a uniform shift r; no estimate is ever sent or compared.
The claim that the eavesdropper's query bound is worst-case (definitions_latex, Definition 2). Both Lemma 3.8 (p. 17) and the proof of Theorem 3.1 (p. 19) bound only the expected number of queries.

"No bound is imposed on ... the output length m(κ)" is presented as the paper's position (parameters, m). Theorem 3.1's bound d_A·d_B/λ is indeed m-free, but p. 6 describes the same result as yielding "a poly(d, m) ≤ poly(κ)-query attack", so the paper is not uniformly on the draft's side here.
verify.reason: The problem is genuinely the paper's own and genuinely open: p. 4 poses it verbatim ("extending them to allow imperfect completeness is an intriguing question for future work", said of all the paper's attacks including the CAQB Theorem 3.1), and nothing in Sections 5–8 or the appendices answers it — Section 6's classical-Alice separation is restricted to perfect completeness, and Section 7's barrier is built on Protocol 7.7 (p. 30), which requires both parties to run the quantum algorithm Q, so the draft's central claim that the barrier misses the classical-Alice case holds up. The single most important defect is in the proof sketch: the draft credits Theorem 3.1 to "a quantum heavy-query learner generalising [BMG09]", but Construction 3.7 learns classical ε-heavy queries for Alice via Lemma 3.6 ("Bounding the classical heavy queries") and Lemma 3.8's argument "identical to" [BM17] — the quantum learner is p. 5's contribution to Theorem 1.3, a different theorem about a different party structure. Combined with the worst-case-versus-expected query bound, the Conjecture 7.1/7.2 slip, and the dropped "infinite set of κ" caveat on Theorem 7.6, these are all locatable and repairable without touching what a proof would have to establish.
